\begin{itemize}
\item This slide is the whole talk; you can come back to it at any point.
\item DNB raised the buffer twice, to two percent, while the Basel reference indicator, the credit-to-GDP gap, pointed to zero.
\item The three boxes answer the three questions of the assignment: environment, criteria and risks, implications.
\item Our verdict: \textbf{normalisation, not tightening}. DNB was refilling a buffer, not fighting a credit boom.
\item The cost to banks was small, it was largely offset by cutting other buffers, and we see \textbf{no sign of a contraction in lending}.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]

\item Credit-to-GDP gap at the decisions: −33pp and −47pp → Basel guide 0\%

\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{CCyB:} Countercyclical capital buffer. Extra bank capital (0–2.5\% of risk-weighted assets) built in good times, released in bad times.
\item \textbf{Credit-to-GDP gap:} How far credit/GDP is above its long-run trend; the Basel starting point for the CCyB.
\item \textbf{O-SII:} "Other systemically important institution". The O-SII buffer is an extra capital charge on large banks.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 3/24 · March 2020\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:30 · from 1:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=3,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item March 2020: COVID hits Europe. Within three weeks, a string of countries \textbf{release} their countercyclical buffers, telling banks to use that capital to keep lending.
\item Sweden and Norway had been at 2.5 percent, the maximum normally used. Denmark, Ireland and Lithuania were at one percent. Germany and Belgium cancelled increases that had been announced but not yet applied.
\item The Netherlands could not do this. Its buffer was at \textbf{zero}, so there was \textbf{nothing to release}.
\item So DNB improvised. On 17 March 2020 it cut the systemic buffers of ING, Rabobank and ABN AMRO and postponed a planned floor on mortgage risk weights. Together that freed about eight billion euros.
\item And it made a promise \emph{(pause)}: once things were back to normal, it would rebuild this capital as a two-percent countercyclical buffer. The whole story turns on that promise.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Releases (rate in force → new rate):
\begin{itemize}
\item Denmark 1.0\% → 0\% (12 Mar)
\item Norway 2.5\% → 1.0\% (13 Mar)
\item Sweden 2.5\% → 0\% (16 Mar)
\item Lithuania 1.0\% → 0\% (31 Mar)
\item France 0.25\% → 0\% (1 Apr)
\item Ireland 1.0\% → 0\% (1 Apr)
\end{itemize}
\item Cancelled pending increases: Belgium 0.5\% (27 Mar) · Germany 0.25\% (31 Mar)
\item Also: Iceland 2.0\% → 0\% · Czech Republic 1.75\% → 1.0\%
\item NL: systemic buffers 3\% → 2.5\% (ING) / 2\% (Rabo) / 1.5\% (ABN AMRO); €8bn freed (incl. the floor postponement); up to €200bn of lending
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Release:} The authority lowers the CCyB rate with immediate effect, so banks may use that capital to absorb losses and keep lending.
\item \textbf{Systemic (risk) buffer:} A structural capital charge on large banks; not designed to be released.
\item \textbf{Mortgage risk-weight floor:} A minimum average risk weight on Dutch mortgages for banks using internal models.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Why does it matter \emph{which} buffer you hold?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 4/24 · The releasable layer\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 2:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=4,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Not all capital is usable in a crisis. Read the stack from the bottom.
\item First come \textbf{requirements} that must always be met: the legal minimum and the bank-specific Pillar 2 requirement.
\item On top sits the \textbf{combined buffer}: the conservation buffer, the systemic buffer and the CCyB.
\item The red dashed line is the MDA trigger. A bank whose capital falls below the top of the combined buffer automatically faces limits on dividends and bonuses. So banks avoid dipping into buffers, even when allowed to; markets punish it.
\item The CCyB is the only layer the authority can \textbf{switch off}. When it is released, the requirement itself falls, and there is no stigma.
\item In COVID, ECB research found that banks close to the MDA trigger cut lending anyway. Only explicitly released capital really works.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Pillar 1 minimum 4.5\% CET1 · capital conservation buffer 2.5\%
\item CCyB 0–2.5\% of RWA (higher possible) · increases bind after 12 months · releases are immediate
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{RWA:} Risk-weighted assets. Assets weighted by riskiness (a mortgage counts less than a corporate loan).
\item \textbf{CET1:} Common Equity Tier 1. The highest-quality capital (shares, retained earnings), as \% of RWA.
\item \textbf{MDA:} Maximum distributable amount. The cap on payouts that applies once capital falls below the combined buffer requirement.
\item \textbf{Pillar 2 requirement / guidance:} The supervisor's bank-specific add-on (binding) / extra expectation (non-binding).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Two years later DNB filled exactly that layer, and the timing looks strange."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 5/24 · The question\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 3:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=5,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item In 2022 DNB keeps its promise, but look at the timing on the left: war in Ukraine, record energy prices, 11.6 percent inflation, ECB rate hikes, house prices about to turn. And the Basel indicator says zero.
\item Raising capital requirements in a downturn is \emph{procyclical}: it amplifies the cycle. That is exactly the mistake the CCyB was invented to prevent.
\item So our question is: \textbf{was this the wrong moment?}
\item We answer in three acts, the three questions of the assignment. The boxes show what each act covers, without overlap: the setting, the decision, the consequences.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item HICP inflation 11.6\% (2022) · ECB first hike 21 Jul 2022 (+50bp)
\item Credit-to-GDP gap −33pp (data to 2021Q4) and −47pp (data to 2022Q4)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Procyclical:} Policy that reinforces the cycle (tighter in bad times, looser in good times).
\item \textbf{Basel buffer guide:} Gap below 2pp → 0\% buffer; above 10pp → 2.5\%; linear in between.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Act 1, the setting. First, the timeline."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 6/24 · Timeline\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 4:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=6,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item The path was set in March 2020 with the promise.
\item In December 2020 the systemic risk buffer was folded into O-SII buffers under new EU rules, and in January 2022 the mortgage risk-weight floor finally came into force.
\item In February 2022 DNB published its new CCyB framework. In May 2022 it announced one percent, just before the ECB began to hike in July. In May 2023 it announced two percent, together with lower O-SII buffers.
\item Both changes became binding on the same day, 31 May 2024, and DNB has held the buffer at two percent every quarter since.
\item Looking ahead: the mortgage floor expires at the end of November 2026.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item 17 Mar 2020 · 29 Dec 2020 · 1 Jan 2022 · Feb 2022 · 25 May 2022 · 31 May 2023 · 31 May 2024 · 30 Nov 2026
\item ECB hikes: first on 21 Jul 2022; still hiking on 14 Sep 2023
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Announcement vs binding date:} Banks get 12 months between a CCyB increase being announced and having to meet it.
\item \textbf{CRD V:} The 2019 revision of the EU Capital Requirements Directive; it made the O-SII and systemic risk buffers additive, prompting DNB's conversion.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 7/24 · Macro\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:05 · from 5:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=7,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item By the third quarter of 2021, Dutch GDP was back above its pre-COVID level; by the end of 2021 it was almost three percent larger than at the end of 2019. That recovery is the condition DNB's framework requires before building the buffer.
\item Then the storm. DNB's spring 2022 Financial Stability Report: "the economic outlook has worsened due to the war in Ukraine and high inflation."
\item Energy prices hit records, inflation reached 11.6 percent, and on 21 July 2022 the ECB raised rates by fifty basis points, its first hike.
\item DNB also warned that higher funding costs would weigh on the debt sustainability of governments, firms and households.
\item So the macro picture argued both ways: build now while the economy can take it, or wait because it is weakening.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]

\item HICP 11.6\% in 2022 (national CPI 10.0\%)
\item ECB +50bp on 21 Jul 2022
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{HICP:} Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, the euro-area-comparable inflation measure.
\item \textbf{Basis point (bp):} 0.01 percentage point; 50bp = 0.5pp.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 8/24 · Credit and housing\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:15 · from 6:35
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=8,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Left panel, \textbf{housing was hot}. In early 2022 nominal house prices rose 19 percent year on year, and real prices were 16 percent above their 2007 peak. DNB itself called the housing market "overheated".
\item But watch what happens next: as mortgage rates rose, real prices fell by about nine percent within a year.
\item Middle panel, \textbf{credit was cold}. Household debt is high by international standards, about 107 percent of GDP versus 58 percent in the euro area, but it was falling.
\item Right panel: the household debt-service ratio, the share of income spent on interest and repayments, was at its lowest since 2005.
\item If there was a boom, it was in house prices, not in credit.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Nominal house prices +19.0\% y/y (2022Q1); real index 129 vs 2007 peak 111 (+16\%)
\item Real house prices −9.2\% (2022Q2–2023Q2)
\item Household debt/GDP: 110\% (2019Q4) → 107\% (2022Q1) → 100\% (2023Q1); euro area 57.7\% (2022Q1)
\item Debt-service ratio, households: 14.6\% (2022Q1)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Debt-service ratio:} Interest plus principal payments as a share of income.
\item \textbf{Real house prices:} Nominal prices deflated by consumer prices.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]

\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 9/24 · Banks\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:05 · from 7:50
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=9,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item The banks were in good shape. The core capital ratio was 17.7 percent at the end of 2021, above the EU average, and 16.3 percent a year later.
\item In DNB's 2023 stress test the four major banks would lose 3.8 points of capital and still end at 11.5 percent, above the 8 percent minimum.
\item And rising rates were lifting profits: net interest income grew 6.7 percent in 2022. DNB wrote that higher rates "may ultimately have a positive impact on the profitability of financial institutions". Keep that sentence in mind; it is our twist later.
\item The bottom row is Act 1 in one line: against raising now, war, inflation, rate hikes and a turning housing market. For raising now, a recovered economy, cold credit and strong, increasingly profitable banks.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item CET1 17.7\% (end-2021; EU 15.7\% in 2021Q3) → 16.3\% (end-2022, in line with EU)
\item Stress test (FSR 2023): −3.8pp → 11.5\% at end-2025 (min. 8\%)
\item Net interest income +6.7\% in 2022; 67.7\% of bank income
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Stress test:} A simulation of a severe recession to check whether capital stays above the minimum.
\item \textbf{Net interest income:} Interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and funding.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ \textbf{\textcolor{nlred}{\textbf{HAND-OVER}}:} "That was the setting. Diego will now show what DNB looked at, and what it was insuring against."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 10/24 · Why not the Basel rule?\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 8:55
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=10,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Thank you. Let me start with the rule DNB chose \emph{not} to follow.
\item The red line is the credit-to-GDP gap, credit relative to its long-run trend. The trend is estimated with a statistical smoother, the Hodrick-Prescott filter. Our own calculation matches the official BIS series almost exactly.
\item On Dutch data, the rule failed three times. It \textbf{missed} the financial crisis: minus 13 points in 2007. It raised a \textbf{false alarm} in 2012, during a house-price bust, because falling GDP inflated the ratio. And it gets \textbf{revised}: 2016 read slightly negative in real time but plus 27 with today's data.
\item Why so bad? Dutch credit rose from under 50 percent of GDP in the 1960s to around 350 percent at its 2015 peak. The filter treats that structural deepening as trend, so once the ratio falls the gap turns deeply negative.
\item At the two decisions it read minus 33 and minus 47 points, so the rule said zero. DNB had good reason to use a different compass.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Gap: −13.4pp (2007Q4) · +16.8pp (2012Q2) · 2016Q1 −0.6pp real time vs +26.9pp ex post
\item −32.7pp (2021Q4) and −46.8pp (2022Q4) at the decisions
\item Credit/GDP 47\% (1961) → 352\% (2015Q1 peak)
\item Replication error ≤ 0.00005pp (1971–2026)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{HP filter:} Splits a series into a smooth trend and a cycle; λ = 400,000 for credit cycles.
\item \textbf{One-sided vs two-sided filter:} One-sided uses only data up to each date (what policymakers see); two-sided also uses later data (hindsight).
\item \textbf{False alarm / missed crisis:} Type II / type I errors of an early-warning indicator.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "So DNB used a different compass."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 11/24 · DNB's framework\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 10:10
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=11,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item That compass is DNB's 2022 framework, with four phases.
\begin{itemize}
\item After a crisis, the buffer is released.
\item In normal times it should be at two percent, built up one point a year.
\item Only when risks are clearly elevated does it go above two percent.
\item In a crisis it is released.
\end{itemize}
\item This is called a \emph{positive neutral} buffer: already filled when risks are neither high nor low.
\item Two percent is calibrated on history: Dutch banks' peak accumulated losses in past crises were about 12 billion euros. Two percent equals about six billion of releasable capital, and releasing it could support up to 150 billion of lending.
\item DNB decides by \emph{guided discretion}: a dashboard of indicators informs the decision but does not dictate it. It also chose two percent "taking into account the buffer reduction in March 2020".
\item The Netherlands is not alone: seventeen jurisdictions run such a framework; Sweden, the UK and Poland also target two percent.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Peak accumulated losses €12bn (2007–2016) → 2\% ≈ €6bn → up to €150bn of lending
\item Build-up: 1pp per year → 2\% after two years
\item 17 jurisdictions with a positive neutral CCyB (BCBS 2024); ECB loss-based range 1.1–1.8\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Positive neutral CCyB:} A CCyB kept above zero in a "standard" risk environment.
\item \textbf{Peak accumulated losses:} The largest cumulative loss a bank suffered over a crisis period.
\item \textbf{Guided discretion:} Decisions informed by a published set of indicators, with judgement, not a formula.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "What reasons did DNB actually give?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 12/24 · DNB's reasons\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:00 · from 11:25
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=12,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{In 2022,} DNB wrote: "When the systemic risk buffers were lowered in March 2020, we also announced our intention to restore the buffers by raising the CCyB." It cited the strong recovery, described risks as "normal to elevated", and acknowledged the uncertainty of the war.
\item \textbf{In 2023,} it said explicitly that the credit gap shows "no signs of excessive credit growth". The reasons it cited: investors' rising risk appetite, falling real-estate prices, debt sustainability of firms and governments, and banks made more robust by higher rates.
\item In neither decision was credit growth the reason. Both rest on a normal-to-elevated risk picture, strong banks and the promise.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item 1\% step: about €3.3bn of extra CET1 (announced 25/27 May 2022)
\item 2\% step: about €3.4bn (announced 31 May 2023)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Cyclical systemic risk:} Risk that builds up over the financial cycle (credit, asset prices, risk-taking) and can materialise system-wide.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "So which risks was the buffer meant to cover?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 13/24 · Risks and tools\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 12:25
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=13,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item DNB's reports name the financial-stability risks, and each was matched to a tool.
\item \textbf{Shocks nobody can forecast} go to the CCyB, because it can be released whatever the source: the war, an energy shock, a sudden tightening of financial conditions, debt-sustainability problems, or bank turmoil abroad such as SVB and Credit Suisse in 2023.
\item \textbf{The known hot spot, housing,} went to other tools: limits on loan-to-value and loan-to-income, tax reform, and the mortgage risk-weight floor.
\item \textbf{The size of the big banks} goes to the O-SII buffer. The sector shrank from about 400 to 280 percent of GDP, which is why that buffer was cut.
\item This is the Tinbergen principle: one instrument per target. DNB itself said more releasable capital is valuable "given the sensitivity of the Dutch economy to external events".
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Banking sector: ≈ 400\% of GDP (when O-SII buffers were phased in) → 280\% (end-2022)
\item Risk-weight floor in force Jan 2022 – Nov 2026
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{LTV / LTI:} Loan-to-value / loan-to-income. Caps on mortgage size relative to house value or income.
\item \textbf{Tinbergen principle:} Reach each policy target with its own instrument.
\item \textbf{Borrower-based measures:} Rules on borrowers (LTV, LTI) rather than on bank capital.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "Now we can test our two suspects."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 14/24 · The verdict\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:30 · from 13:40
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=14,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Was DNB fighting overheating or normalising? Each makes different predictions. Row by row:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Indicators.} Overheating says the buffer rises with them. In fact they all fell while the buffer went up.
\item \textbf{Path.} Normalisation says one point a year, stop at two. That is exactly what happened.
\item \textbf{2023.} House prices were falling and rates jumping. An overheating fighter would pause; DNB raised anyway.
\item \textbf{2024–26.} House prices rose again, about ten percent a year by early 2026. An overheating fighter would go above two percent; DNB held at two.
\item \textbf{Other buffers.} Normalising means cutting structural buffers to compensate. DNB did, twice.
\end{itemize}
\item \emph{(pause)} Five predictions, five matches.
\item The strongest evidence against us is house prices at plus 19 percent in 2022. But DNB used other tools for housing, and when house prices fell, it raised the buffer anyway.
\item That last row is the key to the whole story.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Gap, debt-service ratio and household debt ratio all falling in 2022–23
\item House prices +10\% y/y (DNB, Mar 2026) · CCyB held at 2\% since May 2024
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Phase 3 ("increased risk"):} The framework phase in which the CCyB goes above 2\%.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "Here is what that last row means in euros."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 15/24 · A swap, not a squeeze\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 15:10
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=15,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item This waterfall is our own approximate calculation.
\begin{itemize}
\item In 2020 the systemic-buffer cut released about six billion euros of required capital.
\item The CCyB then added 3.3 billion in 2023 and 3.4 billion in 2024.
\item In 2024 the O-SII cut released another 2.7 billion.
\end{itemize}
\item Net, relative to before COVID: roughly unchanged, if anything slightly lower.
\item DNB said the same: the 2020 plan would be "more or less capital-neutral", and in 2023 Governor Knot spoke of "a limited increase in the net capital requirements".
\item Two caveats. The bases differ: the cuts apply to big banks' worldwide assets, the CCyB to all banks' Dutch exposures. And measured from 2021, not 2019, there was a modest increase.
\item So capital was \textbf{moved}, from buffers that cannot be released into one that can. The UK did something similar.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item −6.0 (2020: ING 1.7, Rabo 2.4, ABN 1.9) · +3.3 (May-23) · +3.4 (May-24) · −2.7 (May-24 O-SII) → net ≈ −2.0 €bn vs pre-COVID
\item Valued at end-2022 total RWA; BNG excluded
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Structural buffer:} A capital charge for permanent features (size, interconnectedness), kept through the cycle.
\item \textbf{UK approach:} The UK offset its 2\% neutral CCyB by lowering Pillar 2A and resolution requirements.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "But even a swap has a cost, especially in a storm. So, was it the wrong moment?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 16/24 · The twist\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 16:25
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=16,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Here is the twist: the storm made it the \textbf{cheapest} moment.
\item Headroom is the capital a bank holds above its requirement. The left panel shows it by bank: ING and Rabobank each had over ten billion euros, ABN AMRO about seven.
\item In total the four banks had about 36 billion at the end of 2022. The full two-percent buffer is 6.7 billion, at most about a fifth, and that is an upper bound.
\item Why so cheap? Rising rates lifted net interest income, so banks could build the buffer from retained earnings instead of cutting loans. Headroom shrank between 2021 and 2022 because risk-weighted assets grew and banks paid out capital, not because of the buffer.
\item The ECB agrees: a gradual build-up with profitable banks "limits these economic costs", and activating buffers during the 2022–23 tightening "can mitigate implementation costs".
\item Not the wrong moment. Arguably the right one.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Headroom end-2021 / end-2022 (€bn):
\begin{itemize}
\item ING 16.9 / 12.6
\item Rabobank 15.7 / 14.2
\item ABN AMRO 7.9 / 7.1
\item de Volksbank 1.9 / 1.7
\end{itemize}
\item Total headroom €42.3bn / €35.5bn → CCyB €3.3bn = 8\%, €6.7bn = 19\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Headroom:} CET1 capital above the bank's requirement (its MDA trigger).
\item \textbf{Retained earnings:} Profits kept in the bank instead of being paid out.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "Cheap for banks, but did borrowers pay?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 17/24 · Borrowers\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 17:40
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=17,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item We ran an event study: Dutch lending rates and loan growth compared with five euro-area countries that never changed their buffer (Austria, Finland, Italy, Malta, Luxembourg), around each policy date.
\item How to read it: the red line is the Netherlands minus those countries; zero means no difference. The grey band shows how big differences get by pure chance. We pretend each control country raised its buffer and plot those "fake" effects.
\item Left: Dutch mortgage rates stay inside the band at all three dates. Right: household credit actually grew faster.
\item Honest detail: before 2022 the Netherlands had lagged, so part of that is catch-up.
\item Our claim is modest. With one treated country this is "no sign of contraction", not a causal estimate. DNB's own verdict in September 2026: "no signs of constraints in bank credit supply".
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Dates: May-22 (1\% announced) · May-23 (1\% binding, 2\% announced) · May-24 (2\% binding)
\item Bank credit 2022Q1–2026Q1: NL +16.6\% vs euro area +7.9\%; 2019–22: NL +4.3\% vs +11.3\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Event study:} Tracks the difference between treated and control groups before and after an event.
\item \textbf{Placebo test:} Rerun the analysis pretending an untreated country was treated, to see what chance alone produces.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ \textbf{\textcolor{nlred}{\textbf{HAND-OVER}}:} "Cheap, and credit kept flowing. But a buffer reaches beyond Dutch banks and borrowers. Zheng."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 18/24 · Monetary policy\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:05 · from 18:55
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=18,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Thank you. First wider implication: monetary policy.
\item The worry was a \textbf{double squeeze}, the ECB raising rates while DNB raised capital requirements.
\item But Dutch lending rates did not diverge from their peers, and bank profits rose with rates.
\item The ECB argues that early buffers "help monetary policy focus on its primary objective of price stability". Macroprudential policy looks after the financial system so that monetary policy can fight inflation.
\item For a euro-area country this matters even more: one monetary policy for twenty countries, but national macroprudential policy. The CCyB is the Dutch-specific lever, and the insurance if a rate shock goes wrong.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item ECB hiking from Jul 2022 (first +50bp) to at least Sep 2023
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Macroprudential policy:} Policy aimed at the stability of the financial system as a whole.
\item \textbf{Monetary policy:} Interest-rate policy aimed at price stability (ECB, euro area-wide).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Second: borders."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 19/24 · Across borders\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 20:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=19,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Under EU reciprocity, any foreign bank lending into the Netherlands must also hold the Dutch two percent on those loans. That limits leakage, lending simply moving to foreign banks, a known weakness of national capital rules. Lending can still leak to non-banks.
\item And the Netherlands is part of a wider shift, shown in the table: Germany, France, Ireland and Belgium raised their buffers in 2023–24; Portugal and Spain follow in 2026.
\item In 2023, five banking-union countries had positive-neutral frameworks, and the Netherlands had the highest rate.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Germany 0.75\% (Feb 2023) · France 1.0\% (Jan 2024) · Ireland 1.5\% (Jun 2024) · NL 2.0\% (May 2024) · Belgium 1.0\% (Oct 2024) · Portugal 0.75\% (Jan 2026) · Spain 1.0\% (Oct 2026)
\item Positive-neutral rates in 2023: Cyprus 0.5\%, Estonia and Lithuania 1.0\%, Ireland 1.5\%, NL 2.0\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Reciprocity:} Foreign banks apply the host country's CCyB rate to exposures there (mandatory in the EU up to 2.5\%).
\item \textbf{Leakage:} Credit shifting to lenders not covered by the rule (foreign branches, non-banks).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Third: what the Netherlands gained."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 20/24 · Resilience\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 21:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=20,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item In 2020 the Netherlands had no capital that was releasable by design. Today it has about 6.7 billion euros, roughly half of the peak losses after the financial crisis, enough to support up to 150 billion of lending.
\item ECB research shows why that is a good deal: raising requirements in normal times costs very little lending, about 0.1 percent per point, while a release in bad times can boost lending by up to ten percent.
\item And its role is growing. The mortgage risk-weight floor expires at the end of November 2026, and DNB says this "underpins the importance" of the two-percent buffer.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item €0 → €6.7bn releasable · ≈ half of €12bn peak losses · up to €150bn of lending
\item Lang \& Menno (2023): −0.1\% lending per +1pp (normal times) vs up to +10\% per 1pp release (bad times)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{State-dependent effect:} The impact of a policy depends on the state of the economy (small in good times, large in bad times).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Fourth: this is not a clean win."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 21/24 · Critiques\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 22:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=21,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Credibility.} Without a mechanical rule, markets must trust DNB's judgement. That is the classic rules-versus-discretion trade-off: a rule is predictable but can be wrong, as we saw; discretion must be explained every quarter.
\item \textbf{Calibration.} Why two percent? ECB estimates suggest 1.1 to 1.8.
\item \textbf{Untested.} We do not yet know whether banks will lend released capital or hoard it.
\item \textbf{Baseline.} Measured against 2021 rather than 2019, it \emph{was} an increase of 3.3 billion before the O-SII offset.
\item \textbf{Same profits, two claims.} The ECB lists the Netherlands among countries that levied excess-profit taxes on banks in 2022–23, partly the same earnings that fund the buffer.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item ECB loss-based range 1.1–1.8\% vs NL 2\% · +€3.3bn vs 2021 before the O-SII offset
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Rules vs discretion:} The trade-off between predictable formulas and flexible judgement (Kydland \& Prescott 1977).
\item \textbf{Excess-profit levy:} A temporary tax on bank profits seen as windfalls from higher rates.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Let me answer the three questions."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 22/24 · Conclusion\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:30 · from 23:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=22,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Environment:} a recovered economy hit by war, inflation and rate hikes; credit cold; housing hot, then cooling; strong, profitable banks.
\item \textbf{Criteria and risks:} a two-percent normal-times level calibrated on past losses, insuring against shocks no one can forecast. Housing went to other tools; structural buffers were cut in return.
\item \textbf{Implications:} cheap, largely a swap, no sign of contraction, complementary to monetary policy, reciprocated abroad, and 6.7 billion euros now releasable. The price is reliance on discretion.
\item The one idea to take away: this was less about \emph{how much} capital banks hold and more about \emph{which kind}.
\item \emph{(pause)} In March 2020, the Netherlands had nothing to release. \textbf{Next time, it will.} The best time to fill a buffer is when nobody thinks you need it, even in a storm. Thank you; we look forward to your questions.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item 0\% → 2\% · −33 / −47pp gap · ≤ 1/5 of headroom · €6.7bn releasable
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Normalisation:} Returning the buffer to its normal-times level, not reacting to overheating.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]

\begin{itemize}
\item Backup for method questions.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Credit gap:} one-sided and two-sided HP filter (λ = 400,000), plus Hamilton regression filter.
\item \textbf{Headroom:} (CET1 ratio minus requirement) × total RWA, per bank.
\item \textbf{Event study:} two-way fixed effects, three-month bins, placebo inference over five never-treated countries.
\end{itemize}
\item All references are verified.
\end{itemize}
